Highly efficient dissolution of xylan in ionic liquid-based deep eutectic solvents
Haitao Yu · Zhimin Xue ID · Xue Lan · Qiaoling Liu · Ruifen Shi · Tiancheng Mu
Received: 11 March 2020/Accepted: 3 May 2020/Published online: 13 May 2020 © Springer Nature B.V. 2020

Abstract Development of efficient solvents to dis- solve lignocellulose and its main components is of significant importance for the utilization/transforma- tion of lignocellulose. Herein, several ionic liquid (IL)-based deep eutectic solvents (DESs) were pre- pared using four ILs as the hydrogen bond acceptors and four different hydrogen bond donors, including thiourea (TU), N-methylthiourea (NMTU), glycerol (Gly), and ethylene glycol (EG). Using the dissolution of xylan (a typical type of hemicellulose) as the example, it was observed that the synthesized IL- based DESs could efficiently dissolve xylan. ## Introduction With the gradual diminishing of nonrenewable fossil resources (i.e., coal, petroleum, and natural gas), interest has been devoted on the pursuit of alternative resources. In this context, lignocellulose, a renewable and abundant resource, has gained significant attention as the alternative of fossil resources to produce various valuable chemicals and functional materials (Mohanty et al. 2018; Schutyser et al. 2018; Sudarsanam et al. 2019; Sun et al. 2018; Zhang et al. 2017). Generally, to efficiently utilize or convert lignocellulose, its dissolution in some suitable solvent is an important issue.

Traditional organic solvents generally have high volatility to cause environmental problems, and thus they are not good candidate for the dissolution of lignocellulose and its main components (i.e., cellu- lose, lignin, and hemicellulose) although some of them could be utilized to dissolve lignocellulose and its components with the satisfactory solubility (Hao et al. 2015; Huang et al. 2016; Xue et al. 2016). To replace the volatile organic solvents, ionic liquids (ILs) have been utilized as functional green solvents for the dissolution of lignocellulose and its components

owing to the unique advantages of ILs (e.g., extremely low vapor pressure, large liquid range, tunable prop-erties) (Cui et al. 2016; Hallett and Welton 2011). Good solubility of lignocellulose and its components can be achieved using ILs as the solvents (King et al. 2011; Lethesh et al. 2020; Rashid et al. 2016; Swatloski et al. 2002; Xu et al. 2017). For example, Yuan et al. (2019) found that the highest solubility of bamboo hemicellulose in 1-butyl-3-methylimida-zolium halide based-ILs was 18.8 g/100 g (15.8 wt%, in [BMIM]Cl) at 120 °C. Liu et al. (2012) synthesized a series of room temperature ILs, in which cholinium acts as the cation and amino acids as the anions, and the solubility of xylan in these ILs ranged from < 1 to 85 mg g⁻¹ (<0.1-7.8 wt%). In addition, Froschauer et al. (2012) described a possi-bility of selective dissolution of xylan using dialkyl phosphate-related ionic liquids. However, the high viscosity of common used ILs often decreases their capability to dissolve lignocellulose and also limits their large-scale applications.

In recent years, deep eutectic solvents (DESs) have drawn numerous attention (Florindo et al. 2019; Ma et al. 2019; Ruiz-Olles et al. 2019; Smith et al. 2014; Zhang et al. 2012). DESs, composed by two compo- nents: hydrogen-bond donor (HBD) and hydrogen- bond acceptor (HBA), have similar properties like ILs, including low volatility, wide liquid range, non- flammability, and designability, etc. Therefore, DESs have been considered as the alternative of ILs in

diverse applications. Attention on the utilization of DESs to dissolve lignocellulose has been awaken in the past few years. In spite of great progress achieved for dissolution of lignocellulose in DESs, using DESs to dissolve lignocellulose is in its early stage, and the successful cases are still limited (Chen et al. 2018; Francisco et al. 2012; Liu et al. 2019; Lynam et al. 2017; Morais et al. 2018; Soares et al. 2017). Especially on the dissolution of hemicellulose, Morais et al. reported the dissolution of xylan in DES aqueous solutions, and the results showed that the highest xylan solubility (328 ± 29 mg mL⁻¹) was obtained with 66.7 wt% DES aqueous solutions at 80 °C (Morais et al. 2018); Lynam et al. (2017) obtained less than 5 wt% xylan solubility with lactic acid:choline chlo- ride 10:1 mol ratio (LA:CC10:1). Therefore, it is highly desired to develop novel and robust DESs for the dissolution of lignocellulose and its components.

Currently, most of DESs are synthesized using quaternary ammonium salts as the HBAs. Considering that some types of ILs are quaternary ammonium salts, these ILs can be used as special HBAs to prepare DESs. Due to the strong hydrogen-bonding interaction between HBD and ILs (as the HBAs), the melting point and the viscosity of the formed DESs would be potentially decreased compared with the corresponding components (HBDs and ILs). Thus, we deduce that these IL-based DESs by combining the advantages of both ILs and DESs could probably be employed as efficient solvents to dissolve lignocellulose and its components.

On the basis of the above discussion, herein, several IL-based DESs (Fig. 1a) were designed by employing thiourea (TU), N-methylthiourea (NMTU), glycerol (Gly) and ethylene glycol (EG) as the HBDs and four ILs [i.e., 1-butyl-3-methylimidazolium chloride ([BMIM]Cl), 1-ethyl-3-methylimidazolium chloride ([EMIM]Cl), 1-hexyl-3-methylimidazolium chloride ([HMIM]Cl), 1-allyl-3-methylimidazolium chloride ([AMIM]Cl)] as the HBAs. To our delight, the prepared DESs showed good performance on the dissolution of xylan (a typical type of hemicellulose, Fig. 1b). More importantly, the solubility of xylan in these IL-based DESs was highly enhanced in comparison with the results in the corresponding ILs.

## Material and methods ### Material Xylan (from corn cob) (Fig. 1b) was purchased from Beijing Innochem Technology Co., Ltd. (Beijing, China). 1-Butyl-3-methylimidazolium chloride ([BMIM]Cl, 97%), 1-ethyl-3-methylimidazolium chloride ([EMIM]Cl, 98%), 1-hexyl-3-methylimidazolium chloride ([HMIM]Cl, 98%), and 1-allyl-3-methylimidazolium chloride ([AMIM]Cl, 96%) were obtained from Shanghai Macklin Biochemical Co., Ltd (Shanghai, China). Nile red and 4-nitroaniline were purchased from J&K Scientific. Thiourea (TU), N-methylthiourea (NMTU), ethylene glycol (EG), and glycerol (Gly) were purchased from Shanghai Aladdin Biochemical Co., Ltd (Shanghai, China).

Preparation and characterization of DESs In a typical process, ILs as HBA, and TU, NMTU, Gly, and EG as HBD were firstly mixed at a molar ratio of 1:1, 2:1 or 3:1, respectively. These DESs were prepared by mixing the two components in a glass vial with a mechanical stirrer at 500 rpm and 363.15 K until a transparent liquid was obtained. Finally, all DESs were stored under vacuum at 333.15 K for 24 h to remove the contained water.

The melting points of DESs were measured via different scanning calorimetry (DSC) conducted on a Q2000 DSC (TA Instruments Waters LCC, USA) at a heating rate of 10 °C min⁻¹ under nitrogen atmosphere, and all the samples for DSC measurements were sealed in Al pans.

The measurements of densities and viscosities for DESs were performed at different temperature, including 298.15, 308.15, 318.15, and 328.15 K, at atmospheric pressure, using an Anton Paar DMA 5000 M density meter with the accuracy of ± 5 × 10⁻⁶ g cm⁻³ and an Anton Paar AMVn viscosity meter using a falling ball technique with an accuracy of < 0.5%. Note that here, the obtained density and viscosity were the average value of four-time measurement, with a deviation of 0.1%. The ¹H NMR (nuclear magnetic resonance) spectra were taken on a Bruker Avance 400 MHz spectrometer. The decomposition temperatures of the prepared DESs were measured by thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) conducted on a TA Instruments TGA Q500.

Solubilities of xylan in DESs and ionic liquids
The method for measuring the solubility of xylan referred to the method for measuring the solubility of lignin by Liu et al. (2019).

In the first step, ca. 1 g of DES was added to a 20 mL glass flask and placed in an oil bath at 323.15, 333.15, and 343.15 K, respectively. After the temperature was constant, about 30 mg of xylan sample was weighed via an electronic balance (with the precision of 0.0001 g) and added into prepared DESs. After the xylan was completely dissolved, the above process was repeated until the added xylan could not be dissolved completely in 1 h. The solubility of xylan with higher potential deviations could be achieved.

In the second step, ca. 1 g of DES was added to 20 mL glass flask and placed in an oil bath at 323.15, 333.15, and 343.15 K, respectively. After the temperature was constant, about 90% of the xylan obtained in the first step was weighed and added into prepared DESs. After being completely dissolved, the xylan was continually added with an increment size of ca. 5 mg until the xylan could not be dissolved in 1 h. The amount of xylan added was recorded and the solubility was calculated.
In addition, the solubility of xylan in four ionic liquids was also measured according to the above method.
Xylan recovered from DESs

Several DESs with high solubility of xylan were selected to regenerate xylan after dissolution. Firstly, ca. 1 g of xylan was dissolved in ca. 4 g DESs at 343.15 K. After xylan was completely dissolved, xylan was precipitated by adding three volumes of ethanol (as the DESs solution). The precipitated xylan was washed with ethanol and acetone, then the recovered solid was filtered via a sand core filter device with 0.45 µm microporous filter membrane.

## Results and discussion ### Synthesis and characterization of the IL-based DESs

In this work, several IL-based DESs were prepared by simply heating the corresponding ILs (as the HBAs) and HBDs (Fig. 1b) with different IL/HBD molar ratios (2:1, 1:1, 3:1), and the detail procedure had been described in the Experimental section. The synthesized DESs were subsequently characterized by various techniques, including DSC (Fig. 2a), thermogravimetric analysis (TGA, Fig. 2b and S1), H NMR (Figs. 2c and S2), and FT-IR (Figs. 2d and S3). Meanwhile, the viscosity (Tables S1–S4), density (Tables S6–S9), and solvatochromic parameters (Table S11) of these DESs were determined for their applications.

First, DSC experiments (Fig. 2a) were conducted to verify the formation of the DESs. It was found that the melting points of DESs were far below those of the corresponding pure components. For instance, the melting points of [BMIM]Cl and TU were 65 °C and 182 °C, respectively, while the melting point of [BMIM]Cl-TU (2:1) was - 62 °C, indicating that the interaction of hydrogen bonds resulted in the decrease of melting point.

Figure 2b presented TGA curves of the synthesized DESs, which denoted their thermal stability. It showed that the decomposition temperature of most of DESs was above 205 °C, which was much higher than the temperature employed to dissolve xylan, indicating that the synthesized DESs were stable in the process of xylan dissolution.

Furthermore, the intermolecular hydrogen-bond interactions between ILs and HBDs were investigated by ¹H NMR spectra (Fig. 2c) and FT-IR spectra (Fig. 2d). In Fig. 2c, two peaks at 3.74 ppm and 5.50 ppm in ethylene glycol represented –CH₂– and – OH, respectively. When the DES was formed between ethylene glycol and [BMIM]Cl, the H signal in the - OH group showed a chemical shift from 5.50 to 5.73 ppm, indicating the existence of hydrogen-bond interaction between ethylene glycol and [BMIM]Cl. Figure 2d showed that the stretching vibration of O–H of pure ethylene corresponded to the peak at 3402 cm⁻¹, while the FT-IR spectra of DES [AMIM]Cl-EG (2:1) showed a strong broad peak at 3390 cm⁻¹. In the examined IL, [AMIM]Cl showed the best result owing to the smaller size of 1-allyl-3- methylimidazolium cation ([AMIM]+) and its relative lower viscosity (Table S5). The smaller size was beneficial for the interaction between the IL and xylan, while the lower viscosity was helpful for mass transport (Ghaedi et al. 2017; Zhang et al. 2005). Thus, [AMIM]Cl showed the best performance for xylan dissolution, which was consistent with the dissolution of cellulose in [AMIM]-based ILs (Zhang et al. 2005).
Comparison on xylan dissolution in pure ILs and the synthesized DESs

The solubilities of xylan in the synthesized DESs and the corresponding ILs were subsequently compared (Figure S5) to confirm the advantage to form DESs. It was found that the solubilities of xylan in these prepared DESs, especially in the Gly-based DESs and EG-based DESs, were much greater than those in the corresponding individual IL. For example, the xylan solubility in [BMIM]Cl was 1.7 wt% at 70 °C, and Yuan et al. reported that the highest xylan solubility was 18.8 g/100 g (15.8 wt%) IL at 120 °C. Compared with it, the xylan solubilities in [BMIM]Cl-based DESs were greater at the same temperature. And the reason would be discussed in the following sec- tion. Meanwhile, for a specific DES, the xylan solubility increased with the increasing dissolution temperature (Figure S5). Moreover, Morais et al. reported that the highest xylan solubility (328 ± 29 mg mL¯¹) was obtained with DES aque- ous solutions (66.7 wt%) at 80 °C (Morais et al. 2018), Lynam et al. (2017) reported that lactic acid:choline chloride 10:1 mol ratio (LA:CC 10:1) showed low xylan solubility, only less than 5 wt%. Compared with those DESs, IL-based DESs showed higher solubility of xylan, especially for [AMIM]CI- EG (2:1) with the maximum solubility of 40.4 wt% (889 ± 30 mg mL¯¹) at 70 °C.
Effect of ILs in the synthesized DESs on xylan solubility
For the TU-based DESs with a IL/HBD molar ratio of 2:1 [i.e., [BMIM]CI-TU (2:1), [HMIM]CI-TU (2:1) and [AMIM]CI-TU (2:1)], the solubility of xylan in

[AMIM]Cl-TU (2:1) was higher than that in other two DESs at all the three determined temperature (Fig. 3a). It was shown that the xylan solubility was extremely low in [BMIM]Cl-based DESs (less than 3 wt% at 323.15 K and 333.15 K) owing to its too high viscosity (9666.4 MPa s). In comparison, the viscosity of [AMIM]Cl-TU (2:1) was only 110.28 MPa s, which was beneficial for xylan disso- lution. Furthermore, when the IL/HBD molar ratio increased from 2:1 to 3:1, the solubilities of xylan in the three DESs ([BMIM]Cl-TU (3:1), [HMIM]Cl-TU (3:1), and [AMIM]Cl-TU (3:1)) increased to some extent (Fig. 3b) because of the decreased viscosity of DESs with the IL/HBD molar ratio of 3:1 (Table S1). It should be pointed out that [EMIM]Cl-TU-based DESs were not determined because they were gener- ally solid at the examined temperature.

Similarly, for NMTU-based DESs with a IL/HBD molar ratio of 2:1, [AMIM]CI-NMTU (2:1) showed the best performance on xylan dissolution (Fig. 3c) owing to its lowest viscosity (Table S2). However, when the IL/HBD molar ratio increased from 2:1 to 3:1, the solubility of xylan only increased slightly owing to the slight decrease of viscosity (Table S2).

In addition, similar phenomenon was achieved when the HBD was EG or Gly. As shown in Fig. 3e–h, the DESs formed using [AMIM]Cl had higher solu- bility of xylan than other DESs generated using other three ILs. Meanwhile, the solubility of xylan also slightly increased with the increasing IL/HBD molar ratio from 1:1 to 2:1 for EG or Gly-based DESs.

From Fig. 3, it could be concluded that the type of ILs could affect the solubility of xylan, and the solubility of xylan in [AMIM]Cl-based DESs was the highest among the DESs with the same HBD, which was probably caused by the lower viscosity of the [AMIM]Cl-based DESs. Meanwhile, for all the deter- mined DESs, the xylan solubility improved with the increasing dissolution temperature from 323.15 to 343.15 K.

Reasons for the higher solubility in DESs than the corresponding IL

As discussed above, the solubility of xylan was higher in the synthesized DESs than the corresponding IL, which may be caused by two reasons. First, after forming DESs, the viscosities decreased significantly in comparison with the corresponding pure IL (Tables S1–S5). Lower viscosity was beneficial for xylan dissolution. Second, the β values of DESs were higher than that of the corresponding pure ILs, indicating that the combination of ILs and HBDs to form DESs could enlarge the hydrogen bond accepting ability, which was helpful to enhance the hydrogen-bond interaction between the solvent and the xylan, and thus the solubility of xylan in the DESs was increased.
Characterization of the regenerated xylan

The dissolved xylan could be easily regenerated from the DESs (employing [EMIM]Cl-NMTU (3:1) as the example) using ethanol as the anti-solvent. Several techniques, including FT-IR spectra, H NMR and C NMR, were conducted to confirm the integrity and purity of the regenerated xylan.

From the FT-IR spectra (Fig. 6), it was observed that the regenerated xylan had similar characteristic bands with the original xylan. For example, the band at 1043 cm⁻¹ was the characteristic absorption of xylan, corresponding to the C–O–C stretching vibration of pyranoid-ring xylans (Morais et al. 2018). Meanwhile, the strong band at 896 cm⁻¹ corresponded to the glyosidic bond β-(1 → 4) between the xylopiranose units of the main xylan chain (Morais et al. 2018),²² while the bands at 1461 and 1375 cm⁻¹ belonged to the stretching peak of –CH₂– and C–O, respectively (Sun et al. 1998). Moreover, the strong absorption peaks at 3384 and 2918 cm⁻¹ were O–H stretching vibration and C–H stretching, respectively. Additionally, the width of the O–H stretching vibration peak (3384 cm⁻¹) of the regenerated xylan narrowed, indicating that the intermolecular and intramolecular hydrogen bonding interactions between xylan were reduced in the process of dissolution and regeneration (Kasprzak et al. 2019; Li et al. 2019).

## Conclusions In summary, several IL-based DESs were designed and synthesized using four ionic liquids as the hydrogen bond acceptors and thiourea, N-methylthiourea, glycerol and ethylene glycol as the hydrogen bond donors. It was found that these synthesized IL-based DESs showed good solubility of xylan, especially for [AMIM]Cl-EG (2:1) with the maximum solubility of 40.4 wt% at 343.15 K compared with those solvents of previous literature. Meanwhile, the xylan solubility was mainly positively correlated with the hydrogen bond accepting ability of DESs. More importantly, the solubility of xylan in these IL-based DESs was much higher than that in the corresponding pure IL owing to the significant decrease of viscosity and the enhanced hydrogen bond accepting ability after the formation of DESs. We believe that the developed DESs have great potential in the separation, dissolution and even conversion of lignocellulose in the future, and formation of DESs is a promising strategy to improve the ability of IL to dissolve biomass, including cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin.

In this context, lignocellulose, a renewable and abundant resource, has gained significant attention as the alternative of fossil resources to produce various valuable chemicals and functional materials (Mohanty et al. 2018; Schutyser et al. 2018; Sudarsanam et al. 2019; Sun et al. 2018; Zhang et al. 2017). Generally, to efficiently utilize or convert lignocellulose, its dissolution in some suitable solvent is an important issue. Traditional organic solvents generally have high volatility to cause environmental problems, and thus they are not good candidate for the dissolution of lignocellulose and its main components (i.e., cellu- lose, lignin, and hemicellulose) although some of them could be utilized to dissolve lignocellulose and its components with the satisfactory solubility (Hao et al. 2015; Huang et al. 2016; Xue et al. 2016). To replace the volatile organic solvents, ionic liquids (ILs) have been utilized as functional green solvents for the dissolution of lignocellulose and its components owing to the unique advantages of ILs (e.g., extremely low vapor pressure, large liquid range, tunable prop-erties) (Cui et al. 2016; Hallett and Welton 2011). Good solubility of lignocellulose and its components can be achieved using ILs as the solvents (King et al. 2011; Lethesh et al. 2020; Rashid et al. 2016; Swatloski et al. 2002; Xu et al. 2017). For example, Yuan et al. (2019) found that the highest solubility of bamboo hemicellulose in 1-butyl-3-methylimida-zolium halide based-ILs was 18.8 g/100 g (15.8 wt%, in [BMIM]Cl) at 120 °C. Liu et al. (2012) synthesized a series of room temperature ILs, in which cholinium acts as the cation and amino acids as the anions, and the solubility of xylan in these ILs ranged from < 1 to 85 mg g⁻¹ (<0.1-7.8 wt%). In addition, Froschauer et al. (2012) described a possi-bility of selective dissolution of xylan using dialkyl phosphate-related ionic liquids. However, the high viscosity of common used ILs often decreases their capability to dissolve lignocellulose and also limits their large-scale applications. In recent years, deep eutectic solvents (DESs) have drawn numerous attention (Florindo et al. 2019; Ma et al. 2019; Ruiz-Olles et al. 2019; Smith et al. 2014; Zhang et al. 2012). DESs, composed by two compo- nents: hydrogen-bond donor (HBD) and hydrogen- bond acceptor (HBA), have similar properties like ILs, including low volatility, wide liquid range, non- flammability, and designability, etc. Therefore, DESs have been considered as the alternative of ILs in <::logo: Springer Springer Black text with a chess knight symbol to its left::> Cellulose (2020) 27:6175–6188 6177 diverse applications. Attention on the utilization of DESs to dissolve lignocellulose has been awaken in the past few years. In spite of great progress achieved for dissolution of lignocellulose in DESs, using DESs to dissolve lignocellulose is in its early stage, and the successful cases are still limited (Chen et al. 2018; Francisco et al. 2012; Liu et al. 2019; Lynam et al. 2017; Morais et al. 2018; Soares et al. 2017). Especially on the dissolution of hemicellulose, Morais et al. reported the dissolution of xylan in DES aqueous solutions, and the results showed that the highest xylan solubility (328 ± 29 mg mL⁻¹) was obtained with 66.7 wt% DES aqueous solutions at 80 °C (Morais et al. 2018); Lynam et al. (2017) obtained less than 5 wt% xylan solubility with lactic acid:choline chlo- ride 10:1 mol ratio (LA:CC10:1). Therefore, it is highly desired to develop novel and robust DESs for the dissolution of lignocellulose and its components. Currently, most of DESs are synthesized using quaternary ammonium salts as the HBAs. Considering that some types of ILs are quaternary ammonium salts, these ILs can be used as special HBAs to prepare DESs. Due to the strong hydrogen-bonding interaction between HBD and ILs (as the HBAs), the melting point and the viscosity of the formed DESs would be potentially decreased compared with the corresponding components (HBDs and ILs). Thus, we deduce that these IL-based DESs by combining the advantages of both ILs and DESs could probably be employed as efficient solvents to dissolve lignocellulose and its components. On the basis of the above discussion, herein, several IL-based DESs (Fig. 1a) were designed by employing thiourea (TU), N-methylthiourea (NMTU), glycerol (Gly) and ethylene glycol (EG) as the HBDs and four ILs [i.e., 1-butyl-3-methylimidazolium chloride ([BMIM]Cl), 1-ethyl-3-methylimidazolium chloride ([EMIM]Cl), 1-hexyl-3-methylimidazolium chloride ([HMIM]Cl), 1-allyl-3-methylimidazolium chloride ([AMIM]Cl)] as the HBAs. To our delight, the prepared DESs showed good performance on the dissolution of xylan (a typical type of hemicellulose, Fig. 1b). More importantly, the solubility of xylan in these IL-based DESs was highly enhanced in comparison with the results in the corresponding ILs. ## Material and methods ### Material Xylan (from corn cob) (Fig. 1b) was purchased from Beijing Innochem Technology Co., Ltd. (Beijing, China). 1-Butyl-3-methylimidazolium chloride ([BMIM]Cl, 97%), 1-ethyl-3-methylimidazolium chloride ([EMIM]Cl, 98%), 1-hexyl-3-methylimidazolium chloride ([HMIM]Cl, 98%), and 1-allyl-3-methylimidazolium chloride ([AMIM]Cl, 96%) were obtained from Shanghai Macklin Biochemical Co., Ltd (Shanghai, China). Nile red and 4-nitroaniline were purchased from J&K Scientific. Thiourea (TU), N-methylthiourea (NMTU), ethylene glycol (EG), and glycerol (Gly) were purchased from Shanghai Aladdin Biochemical Co., Ltd (Shanghai, China). Preparation and characterization of DESs In a typical process, ILs as HBA, and TU, NMTU, Gly, and EG as HBD were firstly mixed at a molar ratio of 1:1, 2:1 or 3:1, respectively. These DESs were prepared by mixing the two components in a glass vial with a mechanical stirrer at 500 rpm and 363.15 K until a transparent liquid was obtained. Finally, all DESs were stored under vacuum at 333.15 K for 24 h to remove the contained water. The melting points of DESs were measured via different scanning calorimetry (DSC) conducted on a Q2000 DSC (TA Instruments Waters LCC, USA) at a heating rate of 10 °C min⁻¹ under nitrogen atmosphere, and all the samples for DSC measurements were sealed in Al pans. The measurements of densities and viscosities for DESs were performed at different temperature, including 298.15, 308.15, 318.15, and 328.15 K, at atmospheric pressure, using an Anton Paar DMA 5000 M density meter with the accuracy of ± 5 × 10⁻⁶ g cm⁻³ and an Anton Paar AMVn viscosity meter using a falling ball technique with an accuracy of < 0.5%. Note that here, the obtained density and viscosity were the average value of four-time measurement, with a deviation of 0.1%. The ¹H NMR (nuclear magnetic resonance) spectra were taken on a Bruker Avance 400 MHz spectrometer. The decomposition temperatures of the prepared DESs were measured by thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) conducted on a TA Instruments TGA Q500. <::logo: Springer Springer A black outline of a chess knight symbol is placed to the left of the word "Springer".::> 6178 Cellulose (2020) 27:6175–6188 A <::chemical structures : The figure displays two sections. In the first step, ca. 1 g of DES was added to a 20 mL glass flask and placed in an oil bath at 323.15, 333.15, and 343.15 K, respectively. In the second step, ca. 1 g of DES was added to 20 mL glass flask and placed in an oil bath at 323.15, 333.15, and 343.15 K, respectively. After the temperature was constant, about 90% of the xylan obtained in the first step was weighed and added into prepared DESs. After being completely dissolved, the xylan was continually added with an increment size of ca. 5 mg until the xylan could not be dissolved in 1 h. The amount of xylan added was recorded and the solubility was calculated. In addition, the solubility of xylan in four ionic liquids was also measured according to the above method. After xylan was completely dissolved, xylan was precipitated by adding three volumes of ethanol (as the DESs solution). The precipitated xylan was washed with ethanol and acetone, then the recovered solid was filtered via a sand core filter device with 0.45 µm microporous filter membrane. The content of uronic acids in both samples were measured according to the reported method (Bastos et al. 2015; Blumenkrantz and Asboe-Hansen 1973; Morais et al. 2018). Here a maximum p value (0.05) was set and the multiple linear regression was expressed by the following equation: ln S = XYZ_0 + aX + bβ + cπ* (1) where a, b and c are coefficients of each parameter and XYZ₀ is intercept. First, all 3 variables {α, β, π*} were performed a multivariate linear regression to determine the coefficients, if all 3 proved statistically significant (_p_ < 0.05), the correlation was accepted. If _p_ value of one or more values were greater than 0.01, then the 3 "pairs" ({α, β}, {α, π*}, {β, π*}) were then fitted for significance, if one or more values proved statistically significant (_p_ < 0.05), the correlation was accepted. If not, then all three variables ({α}, {β}, {π*}) individually were tested. Once again, if _p_ < 0.05 for all members of one of these sets, then the correlation was accepted. ## Results and discussion ### Synthesis and characterization of the IL-based DESs In this work, several IL-based DESs were prepared by simply heating the corresponding ILs (as the HBAs) and HBDs (Fig. 1b) with different IL/HBD molar ratios (2:1, 1:1, 3:1), and the detail procedure had been described in the Experimental section. In this context, lignocellulose, a renewable and abundant resource, has gained significant attention as the alternative of fossil resources to produce various valuable chemicals and functional materials (Mohanty et al. 2018; Schutyser et al. 2018; Sudarsanam et al. 2019; Sun et al. 2018; Zhang et al. 2017). Generally, to efficiently utilize or convert lignocellulose, its dissolution in some suitable solvent is an important issue. Traditional organic solvents generally have high volatility to cause environmental problems, and thus they are not good candidate for the dissolution of lignocellulose and its main components (i.e., cellu- lose, lignin, and hemicellulose) although some of them could be utilized to dissolve lignocellulose and its components with the satisfactory solubility (Hao et al. 2015; Huang et al. 2016; Xue et al. 2016). To replace the volatile organic solvents, ionic liquids (ILs) have been utilized as functional green solvents for the dissolution of lignocellulose and its components owing to the unique advantages of ILs (e.g., extremely low vapor pressure, large liquid range, tunable prop-erties) (Cui et al. 2016; Hallett and Welton 2011). Good solubility of lignocellulose and its components can be achieved using ILs as the solvents (King et al. 2011; Lethesh et al. 2020; Rashid et al. 2016; Swatloski et al. 2002; Xu et al. 2017). For example, Yuan et al. (2019) found that the highest solubility of bamboo hemicellulose in 1-butyl-3-methylimida-zolium halide based-ILs was 18.8 g/100 g (15.8 wt%, in [BMIM]Cl) at 120 °C. Liu et al. (2012) synthesized a series of room temperature ILs, in which cholinium acts as the cation and amino acids as the anions, and the solubility of xylan in these ILs ranged from < 1 to 85 mg g⁻¹ (<0.1-7.8 wt%). In addition, Froschauer et al. (2012) described a possi-bility of selective dissolution of xylan using dialkyl phosphate-related ionic liquids. However, the high viscosity of common used ILs often decreases their capability to dissolve lignocellulose and also limits their large-scale applications. In recent years, deep eutectic solvents (DESs) have drawn numerous attention (Florindo et al. 2019; Ma et al. 2019; Ruiz-Olles et al. 2019; Smith et al. 2014; Zhang et al. 2012). DESs, composed by two compo- nents: hydrogen-bond donor (HBD) and hydrogen- bond acceptor (HBA), have similar properties like ILs, including low volatility, wide liquid range, non- flammability, and designability, etc. Therefore, DESs have been considered as the alternative of ILs in <::logo: Springer Springer Black text with a chess knight symbol to its left::> Cellulose (2020) 27:6175–6188 6177 diverse applications. Attention on the utilization of DESs to dissolve lignocellulose has been awaken in the past few years. In spite of great progress achieved for dissolution of lignocellulose in DESs, using DESs to dissolve lignocellulose is in its early stage, and the successful cases are still limited (Chen et al. 2018; Francisco et al. 2012; Liu et al. 2019; Lynam et al. 2017; Morais et al. 2018; Soares et al. 2017). Especially on the dissolution of hemicellulose, Morais et al. reported the dissolution of xylan in DES aqueous solutions, and the results showed that the highest xylan solubility (328 ± 29 mg mL⁻¹) was obtained with 66.7 wt% DES aqueous solutions at 80 °C (Morais et al. 2018); Lynam et al. (2017) obtained less than 5 wt% xylan solubility with lactic acid:choline chlo- ride 10:1 mol ratio (LA:CC10:1). Therefore, it is highly desired to develop novel and robust DESs for the dissolution of lignocellulose and its components. Currently, most of DESs are synthesized using quaternary ammonium salts as the HBAs. Considering that some types of ILs are quaternary ammonium salts, these ILs can be used as special HBAs to prepare DESs. Due to the strong hydrogen-bonding interaction between HBD and ILs (as the HBAs), the melting point and the viscosity of the formed DESs would be potentially decreased compared with the corresponding components (HBDs and ILs). Thus, we deduce that these IL-based DESs by combining the advantages of both ILs and DESs could probably be employed as efficient solvents to dissolve lignocellulose and its components. On the basis of the above discussion, herein, several IL-based DESs (Fig. 1a) were designed by employing thiourea (TU), N-methylthiourea (NMTU), glycerol (Gly) and ethylene glycol (EG) as the HBDs and four ILs [i.e., 1-butyl-3-methylimidazolium chloride ([BMIM]Cl), 1-ethyl-3-methylimidazolium chloride ([EMIM]Cl), 1-hexyl-3-methylimidazolium chloride ([HMIM]Cl), 1-allyl-3-methylimidazolium chloride ([AMIM]Cl)] as the HBAs. To our delight, the prepared DESs showed good performance on the dissolution of xylan (a typical type of hemicellulose, Fig. 1b). More importantly, the solubility of xylan in these IL-based DESs was highly enhanced in comparison with the results in the corresponding ILs. ## Material and methods ### Material Xylan (from corn cob) (Fig. 1b) was purchased from Beijing Innochem Technology Co., Ltd.
